question: What's Brennan's liability cap now, after the First Amendment?
source: First Amendment to the Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement (January 15, 2026)
evidence: Section 12.2 of the Agreement is deleted in its entirety and replaced with the following: "Brennan's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed One Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($1,500,000) in any Contract Year."

also.source: Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement - Hollis / Brennan (executed, March 1, 2024)
also.evidence: 12.2 Brennan's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($500,000) in any Contract Year.

also.source: Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement - Hollis / Brennan (executed, March 1, 2024)
also.evidence: The limitations in Sections 12.1 and 12.2 shall not apply to damages arising from a Party's gross negligence or willful misconduct, or from Brennan's breach of Section 6 (Temperature Control).

note: $1,500,000 in any Contract Year. The First Amendment (January 15, 2026) deleted the original Section 12.2 ($500,000) and replaced it; the new cap applies to claims arising on or after January 15, 2026 (Amendment 2.2), so it governs the June 2026 loss (Contract Year 3). Section 12.3 is unchanged: no cap applies to damages from Brennan's breach of Section 6 (Temperature Control), or to gross negligence or willful misconduct.

question: Ostrow Kaplan says Brennan's exposure is capped at $500K under Section 12.2. Is that right?
source: Ostrow Kaplan letter for Brennan responding to the demand (September 2, 2026)
evidence: Section 12.2 of the Agreement provides that Brennan's aggregate liability "shall not exceed Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($500,000) in any Contract Year."

also.source: First Amendment to the Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement (January 15, 2026)
also.evidence: Brennan's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed One Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($1,500,000) in any Contract Year.

also.source: Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement - Hollis / Brennan (executed, March 1, 2024)
also.evidence: The limitations in Sections 12.1 and 12.2 shall not apply to damages arising from a Party's gross negligence or willful misconduct, or from Brennan's breach of Section 6 (Temperature Control).

note: No. Ostrow Kaplan quotes the original Section 12.2, which the First Amendment (January 15, 2026) deleted and replaced with a $1,500,000 per Contract Year cap. And under Section 12.3 (left unchanged by Amendment 2.3) neither cap applies to damages arising from Brennan's breach of Section 6 (Temperature Control), which is the core of Hollis's claim. The $1,228,900.00 claim is under the $1.5M cap anyway.

question: Brennan's counsel says our June 9 notice was late because 9.3 only gives us 48 hours. Were we on time?
source: Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement - Hollis / Brennan (executed, March 1, 2024)
evidence: Customer shall give Brennan written notice of any claim for loss of or damage to Goods within five (5) Business Days after Customer becomes aware of the Excursion or damage, and shall submit its full claim with supporting documents within sixty (60) days after that notice.

also.source: Ostrow Kaplan letter for Brennan responding to the demand (September 2, 2026)
also.evidence: Section 9.3 of the Agreement requires the customer to give notice of any claim "within forty-eight (48) hours of delivery."

also.source: Emails - notice of claim and Logger Data request, June 9 to July 24, 2026
also.evidence: Hollis became aware of the Excursion on June 6.

also.source: Emails - notice of claim and Logger Data request, June 9 to July 24, 2026
also.evidence: We acknowledge receipt of your notice of June 9 regarding Shipment HMS-26-0588.

note: Yes. Section 9.3 runs five (5) Business Days from when Hollis becomes aware of the Excursion, not 48 hours from delivery. Hollis became aware on Saturday, June 6, 2026 (arrival at 9:40 a.m.); five Business Days ran to Friday, June 12; notice was emailed June 9 (with courier copy per Section 19) and acknowledged by Halvorsen June 11. The full claim (July 28) was within 60 days of the notice. Ostrow Kaplan's "forty-eight (48) hours of delivery" is a misquote and also assumes the false June 3 delivery date.
